concerns.text: Concatenating windowed matrices across all subjects before k-means clustering (FR-002) conflates inter-subject variability with intra-subject dynamics. This creates a 'common state space' that may not exist biologically, as the clustering algorithm will prioritize variance between subjects (e.g., head size, signal-to-noise ratio) rather than recurrent temporal patterns. This invalidates the 'dynamic metrics' (dwell time) as a measure of individual brain state stability.

The plan relies on a single correlation test (Pearson/Spearman) between structural metrics and dynamic metrics. With N=50 and multiple comparisons (3 structural x 5 dynamic = 15 tests), the statistical power to detect moderate effect sizes after Benjamini-Hochberg correction is critically low. The plan acknowledges this in 'Power & Sample Size' but offers no mitigation (e.g., dimensionality reduction, composite scores, or permutation testing) other than 'exploratory framing,' which does not validate the null hypothesis.

The sensitivity analysis varies structural threshold density (±5%) but applies this to the *same* underlying dMRI matrix. This tests robustness to thresholding, not to the inherent noise or tractography errors in the dMRI data itself. The research question asks about 'topological properties,' which are highly sensitive to the specific tractography algorithm and parameters used to generate the matrix. Without varying the structural input generation (e.g., different tractography seeds or algorithms), the 'robustness' claim is limited to the thresholding step only.

Calculating 'mean dwell time' for k=5 states assumes that the 5 clusters identified are stable and biologically meaningful across the entire cohort. If the k-means solution is unstable (common in high-dimensional fMRI data), the derived 'dwell time' metric becomes a methodological artifact rather than a physiological measure. The plan lacks a stability check (e.g., silhouette score, consensus clustering) before computing per-subject metrics.
